metadata.title: Examining school context and its influence on teachers: linking Talis 2013 with PISA 2012 student data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD TALIS 2013–PISA 2012 link design, where TALIS teacher and principal questionnaires are linked at the school level to PISA student questionnaire and PISA mathematics achievement for the same schools. The paper reports that the TALIS-PISA link followed international sampling guidelines with target response rates and a target of 150 schools per country, with 1 school leader and 20 teachers per school plus all mathematics teachers in each school. For the school-level student composition variables (e.g., ESCS and PISA mathematics achievement), the authors aggregate PISA student measures to the school level and merge them onto the TALIS teacher dataset; they also note that some school-level truancy means are weighted by the teacher weight (TCHWGT). The manuscript does not provide the exact student weight variable names or replicate-weight procedure, so analysts should consult the TALIS 2013 technical documentation for the appropriate TALIS/PISA weight variables and apply complex survey design adjustments when estimating standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses PISA 2012 mathematics achievement plausible values (PV_MATH_MEAN and PV_MATH_SD are explicitly constructed from PISA plausible values aggregated to the school level), but it does not document the specific PV combining rule or software implementation details. This is a reporting gap because PV handling affects standard errors and point estimates when aggregating to school level. Missing-data handling is also not described, so the robustness of results to missingness cannot be assessed from the paper text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset is the TALIS 2013–PISA 2012 linked design for eight participating countries (Australia, Finland, Latvia, Mexico, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Spain). The TALIS component includes teachers and school principals from lower-secondary schools participating in PISA 2012, using the TALIS-PISA link option with school-level linkage. PISA student measures are aggregated to the school level (e.g., ESCS and mathematics achievement plausible values, plus attitude and truancy indicators) and merged onto the TALIS teacher dataset. The paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the link design and aggregation steps, and it does not specify any further grade-level or item-level filtering beyond TALIS/PISA eligibility definitions.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper links TALIS 2013 teacher/principal survey data to PISA 2012 student data using the TALIS-PISA link option in eight countries (Australia, Finland, Latvia, Mexico, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Spain). The linked dataset aggregates PISA student measures to the school level and merges them with TALIS teacher outcomes, enabling exploratory analyses of how student composition and student attitudes/achievement relate to teachers’ professional development engagement, perceived needs for professional development, teaching practices and beliefs, and teacher self-efficacy. The paper reports that 26,610 teachers were combined with school-level measures aggregated from 103,077 students. Analyses use regression, hierarchical linear models, and multilevel models, including interaction terms between teacher characteristics (e.g., gender, experience, mathematics-teacher indicator) and student measures (e.g., ESCS mean/variability, PISA mathematics achievement mean/variability, attitudes, truancy, and immigration proxies). Results vary substantially by country and often differ by teacher gender and whether teachers teach mathematics. The paper emphasizes that TALIS and PISA are cross-sectional and self-report based for many constructs, so findings are statistical associations rather than causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper using linked TALIS 2013 and PISA 2012 data with regression and multilevel modeling, but it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models. Therefore, ML technique fields are intentionally empty, and main_findings are not populated because the schema’s main_findings table is designed for empirical ML prediction targets with model performance metrics. The paper still provides substantive exploratory results via statistical modeling, which are summarized in outcome_summary.
